title: Probability & Tree Diagrams
description: Calculate probabilities for independent and dependent events using AND/OR rules, tree diagrams and expected frequency, including simple conditional probability.

notes.heading: Basic Probability Language

illustration.alt: A tree diagram showing two trials of picking a counter from a bag, with branches labelled with probabilities for red and blue outcomes.
illustration.caption: Tree diagrams show all possible outcomes of two or more events and the probability of each path.

notes.body:
📌 Definition
Probability measures how likely an event is. It is written as a number between $0$ (impossible) and $1$ (certain).

🔑 Key Concept
For equally likely outcomes:
$$P(\text{event}) = \dfrac{\text{number of favourable outcomes}}{\text{total number of possible outcomes}}$$

An event is something that may happen, such as rolling a $6$ or picking a red card.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Probabilities can be written as fractions, decimals or percentages.
• The probability of an event not happening is $P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)$.
• A sample space is a list of all possible outcomes.

notes.heading: Independent Events and the AND Rule
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Two events are independent when one event does not affect the probability of the other.

🔑 Key Concept
For independent events $A$ and $B$:
$$P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B)$$

💡 Worked Example
A fair dice is rolled and a fair coin is tossed. What is the probability of rolling a $4$ and getting tails?

Step 1: Find each separate probability.
$$P(4) = \dfrac{1}{6}$$
$$P(\text{tails}) = \dfrac{1}{2}$$

Step 2: Multiply because the events are independent.
$$P(4 \text{ and tails}) = \dfrac{1}{6} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{12}$$

✅ Check
The answer is less than each separate probability, which makes sense because both events must happen together.

notes.heading: Dependent Events and Conditional Probability
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Two events are dependent when the first event changes the probability of the second event.

🔑 How it works
For dependent events, the probability of the second event must be calculated after the first event has happened. This is called conditional probability.

💡 Worked Example
A bag contains $3$ red and $2$ blue counters. One counter is picked and not replaced, then another is picked. What is the probability of picking two red counters?

Step 1: Probability of red first.
$$P(\text{red first}) = \dfrac{3}{5}$$

Step 2: After one red is removed, $2$ red and $2$ blue remain. Probability of red second is now:
$$P(\text{red second}) = \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$$

Step 3: Multiply.
$$P(\text{red and red}) = \dfrac{3}{5} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{3}{10}$$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using the original probability of $\dfrac{3}{5}$ for the second pick. The total number of counters changes after the first pick.

notes.heading: Mutually Exclusive Events and the OR Rule
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Two events are mutually exclusive if they cannot happen at the same time.

🔑 Key Concept
For mutually exclusive events $A$ and $B$:
$$P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)$$

💡 Worked Example
A fair dice is rolled once. What is the probability of rolling a $2$ or a $5$?

Step 1: Find each probability.
$$P(2) = \dfrac{1}{6}$$
$$P(5) = \dfrac{1}{6}$$

Step 2: Add because the two outcomes cannot both happen on one roll.
$$P(2 \text{ or } 5) = \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Only add probabilities when the events cannot happen together.
• Rolling a $2$ and rolling a $5$ on one roll are mutually exclusive.
• Picking a red card and picking a heart from a deck are not mutually exclusive because a card can be both red and a heart.

notes.heading: Drawing and Using Tree Diagrams
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A tree diagram is a picture that shows all possible outcomes of two or more events. Each branch is labelled with its probability.

🔑 How it works
• Draw a branch for each possible outcome of the first event.
• From the end of each branch, draw branches for the second event.
• Multiply along branches to find the probability of a combined outcome.
• Add outcomes that answer the question.

💡 Worked Example
A bag contains $2$ red and $3$ blue counters. A counter is picked, replaced, then another is picked. Find the probability of one red and one blue in any order.

Step 1: Because of replacement, the events are independent.
$$P(\text{red}) = \dfrac{2}{5}, \quad P(\text{blue}) = \dfrac{3}{5}$$

Step 2: Two paths give one of each colour: red then blue, or blue then red.
$$P(\text{red then blue}) = \dfrac{2}{5} \times \dfrac{3}{5} = \dfrac{6}{25}$$
$$P(\text{blue then red}) = \dfrac{3}{5} \times \dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{6}{25}$$

Step 3: Add the two paths.
$$P(\text{one of each}) = \dfrac{6}{25} + \dfrac{6}{25} = \dfrac{12}{25}$$

✅ Check
The probabilities of all paths add to $1$:
$$\dfrac{4}{25} + \dfrac{6}{25} + \dfrac{6}{25} + \dfrac{9}{25} = 1$$

notes.heading: Expected Frequency
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Expected frequency is the number of times you expect an event to happen if an experiment is repeated many times.

🔑 Key Concept
$$\text{expected frequency} = \text{probability of event} \times \text{number of trials}$$

💡 Worked Example
A fair coin is tossed $200$ times. How many heads are expected?

Step 1: Probability of heads.
$$P(\text{heads}) = \dfrac{1}{2}$$

Step 2: Multiply by the number of trials.
$$\text{expected heads} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 200 = 100$$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Expecting exactly $100$ heads every time. The actual number may vary, but $100$ is the long-run average.

notes.heading: Simple Conditional Probability
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Conditional probability is the probability of an event happening given that another event has already happened.

🔑 Key Concept
The notation $P(A | B)$ means the probability of $A$ given that $B$ has happened.

💡 Worked Example
A class has $12$ boys and $18$ girls. Half of the boys and one third of the girls wear glasses. A student is chosen at random. Given that the student is a girl, what is the probability she wears glasses?

Step 1: Focus only on the girls because the condition is given.
Number of girls = $18$.
Number of girls with glasses = $\dfrac{1}{3} \times 18 = 6$.

Step 2: Find the conditional probability.
$$P(\text{glasses} | \text{girl}) = \dfrac{6}{18} = \dfrac{1}{3}$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Conditional probability reduces the sample space to only those outcomes that satisfy the condition.
• Tree diagrams are very useful for organising conditional probabilities.

flashcards.definition: Two events are independent when one does not affect the probability of the other.
flashcards.example: Rolling a dice and tossing a coin are independent.

flashcards.definition: Two events are dependent when the first changes the probability of the second.
flashcards.example: Picking counters from a bag without replacement.

flashcards.definition: To find the probability of both events happening, multiply their probabilities.
flashcards.example: $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B)$ for independent events.

flashcards.definition: To find the probability of either of two mutually exclusive events happening, add their probabilities.
Events that cannot happen at the same time.
flashcards.example: Rolling a $2$ and rolling a $5$ on one dice roll.

flashcards.definition: A diagram that shows all possible outcomes of two or more events using branches.
flashcards.example: Each branch is labelled with a probability; multiply along branches.

flashcards.definition: The number of times an event is expected to happen in a given number of trials.
The probability of an event happening given that another event has already happened.
flashcards.example: $P(\text{glasses} | \text{girl})$ means probability of glasses given the student is a girl.

flashcards.definition: A list of all possible outcomes of an experiment.
flashcards.example: For a coin toss the sample space is heads, tails.

flashcards.definition: The probability that an event does not happen.
An item is returned before the next selection, so probabilities stay the same.
flashcards.example: Picking a counter and putting it back makes the events independent.

flashcards.definition: An item is not returned, so the total and probabilities change for the next selection.
flashcards.example: Picking two counters from a bag without replacing the first.

questions.stem: A bag contains $4$ red and $6$ blue counters. One counter is picked at random. What is the probability it is red?
questions.explanation: There are $4$ red counters out of $10$ total, so $P(\text{red}) = \dfrac{4}{10} = \dfrac{2}{5}$.

questions.stem: A fair dice is rolled and a fair coin is tossed. What is the probability of rolling a $5$ and getting heads?
A fair dice is rolled once. What is the probability of rolling an even number or a $3$?
questions.explanation: Even numbers are $2$, $4$, $6$, and adding $3$ gives $4$ favourable outcomes out of $6$: $\dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

questions.stem: A bag has $3$ red and $7$ blue counters. A counter is picked, replaced, then another is picked. What is the probability both are blue?
questions.explanation: Because of replacement the events are independent: $\dfrac{7}{10} \times \dfrac{7}{10} = \dfrac{49}{100}$.

questions.stem: A bag has $3$ red and $7$ blue counters. A counter is picked and not replaced, then another is picked. What is the probability both are blue?
Which formula gives the probability of two independent events both happening?
questions.explanation: For independent events, multiply the probabilities: $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B)$.

questions.stem: A spinner has probability $0.3$ of landing on red. If it is spun $80$ times, how many reds are expected?
questions.explanation: Expected frequency = $0.3 \times 80 = 24$. The actual number may vary but $24$ is the long-run average.

questions.stem: A card is picked from a standard deck. What is the probability it is a heart or a diamond?
questions.explanation: Hearts and diamonds are mutually exclusive suits. $\dfrac{13}{52} + \dfrac{13}{52} = \dfrac{26}{52} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.stem: A tree diagram has two events. The first branch has probability $\dfrac{1}{3}$ and the second branch has probability $\dfrac{1}{4}$. What is the probability of travelling along both branches?
A biased coin has $P(\text{heads}) = 0.6$. It is tossed twice. What is the probability of two heads?
A class has $10$ boys and $20$ girls. One third of the girls have brown eyes. Given that a chosen student is a girl, what is the probability she has brown eyes?
questions.explanation: The condition limits the sample space to girls only. One third of the girls have brown eyes, so the probability is $\dfrac{1}{3}$.

questions.stem: A bag contains $5$ green and $5$ yellow marbles. One marble is picked and not replaced, then another is picked. What is the probability both are green?
Which of these pairs of events are mutually exclusive?
choices: Rolling a $1$ and rolling a $6$ on one dice roll
Rolling an even number and rolling a $2$
Picking a red card and picking a heart
questions.explanation: A single dice roll cannot be both $1$ and $6$, so these are mutually exclusive.
